inconsistencies: Boost.Test replacement cluster: #35713 (full in-tree runner), #35139 (new thread-safe ASSERT macros) and #36091 (operator<< for tested types) overlap in the same space. #36091 is stated groundwork for #35713 and should be reviewed first or together; #35139's macro set may be subsumed by or must be reconciled with #35713's framework, so the approach decision on #35713 should come before merging #35139 broadly.

Benchmark block/undo fixture: #32554 (runtime block+undo generator, supersedes #32457) and #36254 (add static undo data for block 413567) solve the same problem that BlockToJsonVerbosity3 measures nothing. Decide the generator-vs-static-fixture approach once; #36254 is the narrow immediate fix, #32554 the general replacement.
Functional-test speed cluster: #36440, #36439 and #36446 all cut waits in the same framework helpers and will conflict. Review #36440 first (largest measured gain), then #36439, then #36446.

Release-binary CI coverage: #36082 (Guix builds plus unit/functional tests on native runners) would largely subsume #35774 (test cross-built macOS arm64 binaries). Review #35774 first as the narrower change with a concrete caught regression (#35771), then decide whether #36082 replaces it.
#35442 depends on #35433 (replaceable RPC argument deprecation) and currently bundles its commits; it cannot land before that chain resolves.
#34360 exists to measure optimizations proposed in #27865; its value is contingent on that PR being pursued.
#32409 has been NACKed as code that nothing in the repository uses or documents; a decision to close may be more useful than review.
result.notes: No PR in this category is a true release blocker except #36437, which pairs a real relay-liveness fix with the harness that found it. The list otherwise divides cleanly: signal/flake and high-risk coverage work at the top (P2), framework capabilities and measured speedups next, then the long tail of benchmark additions and test-vector contributions (P3), and mechanical or unused cleanups (P4). Several P3 benchmark PRs are individually fine but collectively low-leverage; a reviewer short on time should take them as a batch.
